people.name: Norma Torres
body: Before she wrote laws, Norma Torres answered emergency calls. She began her public service career as a 911 dispatcher in Los Angeles, and her congressional office says she worked from there to improve 911 service for Los Angeles residents. That work on the dispatch floor became the base of a career in public office.

Torres was born on April 4, 1965, in Escuintla, Guatemala. Her congressional office calls her a lifelong resident of Pomona, California. She earned a bachelor's degree in labor studies from the National Labor College in 2012.

Her first elected office was close to home. She served on the Pomona City Council from 2000 to 2006 and as mayor of Pomona from 2006 to 2008. She then served in the California State Assembly from 2008 to 2013 and in the State Senate from 2013 to 2014. As a state senator she wrote legislation to modernize the 9-1-1 system.

Voters elected her to the U.S. House of Representatives in November 2014, and she has served since 2015. Her office describes her as the only Central American-born member of Congress. As of October 2026 she serves on the House Appropriations Committee, where she is a senior member of the subcommittee that handles transportation and housing. Every House seat is on the ballot on November 3, 2026.
keyFacts: April 4, 1965: Born in Escuintla, Guatemala.
2000–2006: Pomona City Council. 2006–2008: Mayor of Pomona.
2008–2013: California State Assembly. 2013–2014: California State Senate.
November 2014: Elected to the U.S. House; serving since 2015.
Described by her office as the only Central American-born member of Congress.
people.connectToWork: When a person calls your service in an emergency, what happens if the first person who answers does not speak their language? Who on your team would know?

people.name: Luis von Ahn
body: Almost everyone online has typed wavy, distorted letters to prove they are human. That test, the CAPTCHA, came from Luis von Ahn and his mentor Manuel Blum at Carnegie Mellon University, where von Ahn earned his doctorate in 2005. Von Ahn later found a way to put that effort to use. His reCAPTCHA system turned millions of tiny typing tasks into help digitizing books. Google bought reCAPTCHA in 2009.

Von Ahn was born and raised in Guatemala City. He came to the United States for his education and became a professor of computer science at Carnegie Mellon in Pittsburgh. His research centered on "human computation," the idea that people's small online actions can be combined to solve problems computers cannot solve alone.

His best-known project grew from a question about who gets access to opportunity. Learning English can open doors to jobs, but language classes cost money that many people do not have. In 2011 von Ahn co-founded Duolingo with Severin Hacker, then a graduate student. Duolingo is a free, game-like language-learning app, and as of October 2026 von Ahn is its chief executive. He was named a MacArthur Fellow in 2006 and a Carnegie Corporation "Great Immigrant" in 2021.
keyFacts: 1978: Born in Guatemala City.
Co-created CAPTCHA with Manuel Blum at Carnegie Mellon; doctorate in 2005.
2006: MacArthur Fellow.
2009: Google acquired reCAPTCHA.
2011: Co-founded Duolingo with Severin Hacker.
2021: Carnegie Corporation "Great Immigrant".
people.connectToWork: Which steps in your process assume a person reads English, or Spanish, well? What would the same step look like for someone whose first language is neither?

people.name: Ted Hendricks
body: At the University of Miami, teammates looked at the tall, thin linebacker and gave him a nickname that stuck: "The Mad Stork." In the NFL he became known simply as "The Stork." Ted Hendricks was a three-time All-American at Miami as a linebacker and defensive end.

Hendricks was born in Guatemala City on November 1, 1947. His mother was Guatemalan, and his parents worked for Pan Am. Hall of Fame accounts describe a family move to Hialeah, Florida, where he grew up. Emisoras Unidas, a Guatemalan outlet, says he lived in Guatemala until he was 18.

The Baltimore Colts drafted him in the second round in 1969. Over 15 seasons he played for the Baltimore Colts (1969–1973), the Green Bay Packers (1974), and the Oakland and Los Angeles Raiders (1975–1983). He played in four Super Bowls: Super Bowl V with the Colts, and Super Bowls XI, XV and XVIII with the Raiders. He used his long reach to block kicks, deflect passes and rush quarterbacks.

The Pro Football Hall of Fame inducted him in 1990. The College Football Hall of Fame has honored him during Hispanic Heritage Month as a Guatemalan-born star. In 2026 he was part of the first class of the Hispanic Football Hall of Fame, and he joked in his speech that people did not believe he was Guatemalan because he was so tall.
keyFacts: November 1, 1947: Born in Guatemala City.
College: University of Miami, three-time All-American.
1969: Drafted in the second round by the Baltimore Colts.
1969–1983: Played for the Colts, Packers and Raiders; four Super Bowls.
1990: Inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame.
2026: First class of the Hispanic Football Hall of Fame.
people.connectToWork: What do you assume about a person's background from how they look, their name or their English? How would your intake change if you asked instead?

people.name: Francisco Goldman
body: In 1998, Bishop Juan Gerardi was killed in Guatemala City. Days earlier he and a group of lawyers had presented a report on human rights abuses committed against civilians by the military during Guatemala's civil war. Francisco Goldman spent years following the investigation and the trial of several military officers that came after. The result was The Art of Political Murder (Grove Press), a book that a judge of a human-rights prize compared to Truman Capote's In Cold Blood.

Goldman was born in Boston in 1954 to a Guatemalan mother and a Jewish American father, and Guatemala runs through much of his work. His first novel, The Long Night of White Chickens, won the 1993 Sue Kaufman Prize for First Fiction from the American Academy and Institute of Arts and Letters and was a PEN/Faulkner Award finalist. It follows a Guatemalan American family's ties to Guatemala City during the war years.

The Art of Political Murder won the first WOLA-Duke Book Award for Human Rights in Latin America in 2008, as well as the Index on Censorship T.R. Fyvel Book Award. His 2021 novel Monkey Boy was a finalist for the 2022 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. Trinity College in Hartford, Connecticut, where he has taught since 2002, described him in 2022 as its Allan K. Smith Professor of English.
keyFacts: 1954: Born in Boston to a Guatemalan mother and Jewish American father.
1993: Sue Kaufman Prize for The Long Night of White Chickens; PEN/Faulkner finalist.
Since 2002: On the faculty at Trinity College.
2008: First WOLA-Duke Book Award for Human Rights in Latin America, for The Art of Political Murder.
2022: Pulitzer Prize finalist in fiction for Monkey Boy.

people.name: Héctor Tobar
body: In spring 1992, Los Angeles burned for days after the acquittal of the police officers who beat Rodney King. Héctor Tobar, the Los Angeles-born son of Guatemalan immigrants, was part of the Los Angeles Times team whose coverage of the riots won a Pulitzer Prize.

Tobar was born in Los Angeles in 1963 and raised there. He studied Latin American studies and sociology at UC Santa Cruz and earned an MFA in creative writing at UC Irvine. At the Times he was national Latino affairs correspondent, bureau chief in Mexico City and Buenos Aires, a columnist and a book reviewer.

His first novel was The Tattooed Soldier (2000), and The Barbarian Nurseries (2011) is set in contemporary Southern California. His nonfiction includes Translation Nation, about Spanish-speaking America, and Deep Down Dark, the New York Times bestseller about the 33 men trapped in a Chilean mine. The book became the basis of the film The 33, starring Antonio Banderas and Juliette Binoche. His book Our Migrant Souls is a meditation on race and the meanings of the word "Latino." Tobar is a professor of English and Chicano/Latino studies at UC Irvine and was named a Guggenheim Fellow in 2023.
keyFacts: 1963: Born in Los Angeles to Guatemalan immigrant parents.
1992: Part of the Los Angeles Times team awarded a Pulitzer Prize for coverage of the Los Angeles riots.
2000: The Tattooed Soldier. 2011: The Barbarian Nurseries.
2012: UCSB Luis Leal Award for Distinction in Chicano/Latino Literature.
2023: Guggenheim Fellowship.
people.connectToWork: Does your form or data system put everyone under one word such as "Latino"? What would you miss about the people you serve because of it?

people.name: Oscar Isaac
body: In Inside Llewyn Davis (2013), Oscar Isaac played the title role, a struggling folk singer in 1960s Greenwich Village. It became one of the defining roles of his career.

Isaac was born on March 9, 1979, in Guatemala City. His mother, María Eugenia Estrada Nicolle, is Guatemalan, and his father, Óscar Gonzalo Hernández-Cano, is Cuban. The family lived in Baltimore and New Orleans before settling in Miami in the mid-1980s. There he played in ska bands as a high school student. He was accepted to the Juilliard School in 2001 and graduated in 2005.

His career covers independent drama and global blockbusters. He played José Ramos-Horta in Balibo (2009), which won him an Australian Film Institute award. He appeared in Drive (2011) and Ex Machina (2014). He played Poe Dameron in Star Wars: The Force Awakens (2015) and Duke Leto Atreides in Dune (2021). He won at the Golden Globes for the HBO miniseries Show Me a Hero (2015), and the Inside Llewyn Davis role earned him a nomination there. He received Emmy and Screen Actors Guild nominations, and another at the Golden Globes, for Scenes from a Marriage (2021), and he starred in Moon Knight (2022).
keyFacts: March 9, 1979: Born in Guatemala City.
2005: Graduated from the Juilliard School.
2013: Title role in Inside Llewyn Davis; nominated at the Golden Globes.
2015: Won at the Golden Globes for Show Me a Hero; Poe Dameron in Star Wars.
2021: Dune and Scenes from a Marriage.
people.connectToWork: If a form lets a person choose only one national origin or ethnicity, who gets left out? What would it take to change the form, or to ask a better question beside it?

people.name: José Antonio Gutiérrez
body: On March 21, 2003, in the first days of the Iraq War, Lance Corporal José Antonio Gutiérrez was killed near the port city of Umm Qasr. He was among the first U.S. service members to die in the war, and he was not yet a U.S. citizen. Military Times reports that he died in a firefight. The Los Angeles Almanac says it was later determined he was killed by friendly fire.

By Military Times's account, Gutiérrez was born in Guatemala City and his parents died when he was young. Accounts of his journey differ. Military Times reports he left at 14 and hopped freight trains through Mexico; his sister told reporters he left at 11 and crossed Mexico alone by train. The Los Angeles Almanac says he left at 17 with another boy and convinced immigration authorities he was 16. He became a ward of the Los Angeles Juvenile Court, settled with a foster family in Lomita, California, and finished high school. He received legal residency after turning 18 and joined the Marine Corps. He served as a rifleman with the 2nd Battalion, 1st Marine Regiment, 1st Marine Division, based at Camp Pendleton.

After his death, at age 22, the U.S. government granted him citizenship posthumously. At the request of his only surviving blood relative, an older sister, he was buried in Los Cipreses Cemetery in Guatemala City. A cenotaph honors him at Los Angeles National Cemetery.
keyFacts: Born in Guatemala City; left young, at 11, 14 or 17 by different accounts.
Ward of the Los Angeles Juvenile Court; foster home in Lomita, California.
1999: Received permanent residency.
Rifleman, 2nd Battalion, 1st Marines, 1st Marine Division.
March 21, 2003: Killed near Umm Qasr, Iraq, at age 22.
Granted U.S. citizenship posthumously; buried in Guatemala City.
people.connectToWork: When a young person arrives without parents, who in your process has the authority to speak for them, and which family ties across a border do you ask about?

people.name: Maya Chinchilla
body: Maya Chinchilla's debut book carries a playful title: The Cha Cha Files: A Chapina Poética. "Chapina" is a word for a Guatemalan woman. Her publisher, Kórima Press, describes the 2014 book as exploring the Central American and Guatemalan diaspora and the aftermath of civil and urban wars. It is a mix of poems, stories and snapshots about feminist and punk communities, families separated by war, and love across borders, set from the California coast to the Bay Area.

Chinchilla is a Guatemalan writer, video artist and educator based in the San Francisco Bay Area. Her poetry explores historical memory, heartbreak, tenderness, sexuality and alternative futures. She earned her undergraduate degree at UC Santa Cruz, where she founded and co-edited the annual publication La Revista, and an MFA in English and creative writing from Mills College.

She co-edited Desde El Epicentro, an anthology of Central American poetry and art. Universities including UC Irvine, UCLA and, in April 2021, the University of Maryland have hosted readings and talks on her work.

people.name: Gaby Moreno
body: Many American television viewers have heard Gaby Moreno without knowing her name. She co-wrote the theme song for NBC's comedy Parks and Recreation and received an Emmy nomination for it. She records in English and Spanish.

Moreno was born María Gabriela Moreno Bonilla on December 16, 1981, in Guatemala. Her grandfather was the grammarian José Bonilla Ruano. She moved from there to Los Angeles, where she built her career as a singer, songwriter and guitarist. In 2006 she won the grand prize in the John Lennon Songwriting Contest.

In 2013 she won the Latin Grammy for Best New Artist. She has toured with or shared stages with artists including Tracy Chapman, Ani DiFranco, Ricardo Arjona, the Punch Brothers and Calexico. In 2019 Nonesuch Records released ¡Spangled!, her collaboration with the songwriter and arranger Van Dyke Parks. Her self-produced album Alegoría (2022) earned a Grammy nomination for Best Latin Rock or Alternative Album. In 2023 she won a second Latin Grammy, as producer of Vida, an album by the Cuban singer Omara Portuondo, and in 2024 she won a Grammy for Best Latin Pop Album for X Mí (Vol. 1). In December 2024 Guatemala's president gave her the Orden Presidencial.
keyFacts: December 16, 1981: Born in Guatemala; later moved to Los Angeles.
2006: Grand prize, John Lennon Songwriting Contest.
Emmy nomination for co-writing the Parks and Recreation theme.
2013: Latin Grammy for Best New Artist. 2023: Latin Grammy as producer of Vida.
2024: Grammy for Best Latin Pop Album (X Mí, Vol. 1).

people.name: Arturo Arias
body: In the mid-1980s, American audiences watched El Norte, a film about Guatemalans fleeing north to the United States. Guatemalan novelist Arturo Arias co-authored its screenplay, according to his published biographies.

Arias was born in Guatemala City on June 22, 1950. He earned a doctorate in the sociology of literature from the École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales in Paris. His novels in Spanish include Después de las bombas (1979; in English, After the Bombs, 1990), Itzam Na (1981), which won the Casa de las Américas prize, Jaguar en llamas (1989) and Cascabel (1998; in English, Rattlesnake, 2003).

Arias built much of his career in American universities. He taught at San Francisco State University and directed Latin American studies at the University of Redlands. UC Santa Barbara's Global Latinidades project lists him as the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Endowed Professor in Humanities at UC Merced. He served as president of the Latin American Studies Association from 2001 to 2003. His scholarship includes The Rigoberta Menchú Controversy (2001) and Taking Their Word: Literature and the Signs of Central America (2007), both published by the University of Minnesota Press.

In 2008 Guatemala gave him its Miguel Ángel Asturias National Prize for lifetime achievement in literature. In 2020 he received a Guggenheim Fellowship for his trilogy Recovering Lost Footprints, which studies contemporary Indigenous literature from Guatemala and Mexico.
keyFacts: June 22, 1950: Born in Guatemala City.
Doctorate in the sociology of literature, École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales, Paris.
Co-authored the screenplay of El Norte.
2001–2003: President of the Latin American Studies Association.
2001 and 2007: Books published by the University of Minnesota Press.
2008: Miguel Ángel Asturias National Prize in Literature. 2020: Guggenheim Fellowship.

people.name: Delia Ramirez
body: Delia Ramirez represents Illinois's 3rd District in the U.S. House of Representatives. Her congressional office describes her as the first Latina elected to Congress from Illinois and from the entire Midwest. It also calls her the only member of Congress who belongs to a mixed-status family, a family in which some relatives have legal immigration status and some do not.

Ramirez was born on June 2, 1983, in Chicago, in the Belmont Cragin community, and is a lifelong resident of the city's Humboldt Park neighborhood. Her office describes her as the daughter of working-class Guatemalan immigrants who both worked low-wage jobs. She graduated from Northeastern Illinois University with a degree in justice studies.

Before she ran for office she spent about 18 years in Chicago's nonprofit sector. She was executive director of the Center for Changing Lives, campaign manager for Common Cause Illinois, and deputy director of the Community Renewal Society. She also chaired the boards of two neighborhood groups, the Latin United Community Housing Association (LUCHA) and the Logan Square Neighborhood Association.

In 2018 she ran for the Illinois House of Representatives in the 4th District, and she won. The Illinois House Democrats describe her as the first Guatemalan American to serve in the Illinois General Assembly. In Springfield she co-founded the Illinois House Progressive Caucus and became an assistant majority leader.

Her first U.S. House term began on January 3, 2023. As of October 2026 she serves on the Committee on Homeland Security and the Committee on Veterans' Affairs, where her office says she is the top Democrat on the Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations. Every House seat is on the ballot on November 3, 2026.
keyFacts: June 2, 1983: Born in Chicago to Guatemalan immigrant parents.
About 18 years in Chicago nonprofit leadership.
2018: Elected to the Illinois House; first Guatemalan American in the Illinois General Assembly, by the Illinois House Democrats' account.
Since January 3, 2023: U.S. House, Illinois's 3rd District.
people.connectToWork: If someone in a household fears a relative's immigration status could be exposed, what does your process ask for that they might avoid giving? What can you tell them, accurately, about who sees it?

people.name: Manny Marroquin
body: Manny Marroquin was born in Guatemala. When he was nine, his family moved to Los Angeles because of Guatemala's civil war. He has recalled how central music was in Guatemala when he was very young, telling Grammy.com that "music is a huge part" of life in poor countries like it.

At Alexander Hamilton High School in Los Angeles he spent long hours in the school's recording studio, and an electronic music class there pointed him toward mixing. On a teacher's advice he turned down college scholarship offers to take an entry-level runner job at Enterprise Studios, where he worked his way up to engineering. His break came when a producer heard a late-night rough mix he had made and gave him a whole album to mix.

He is based at Larrabee Studios in Los Angeles. As a mix engineer he has worked on records by Kanye West, Alicia Keys, John Legend, Taylor Swift, Beyoncé, Lizzo and many others. Grammy.com has called him an eight-time Grammy winner. His own site, using later figures, gives a running total of 18 Grammy Awards and lists four Latin Grammy Awards, three of them for Rosalía's Motomami.
keyFacts: Born in Guatemala; family moved to Los Angeles when he was nine because of the civil war.
Started as a runner at Enterprise Studios after high school.
Based at Larrabee Studios, Los Angeles.
Grammy totals differ by source and date: eight per Grammy.com, 18 per his own site.

people.name: Rebecca Balcárcel
body: Twelve-year-old Quijana is half Latina and half Anglo. She does not speak Spanish and does not want to go to Guatemala for winter break, and she cannot tell whether she is happy being half. She is the heroine of The Other Half of Happy (Chronicle Books, 2019), the first middle-grade novel by Rebecca Balcárcel. The book received a 2020 Pura Belpré Author Honor from the American Library Association and REFORMA.

Balcárcel was born in Iowa to a Guatemalan father and a mother born in Iowa to a family of British descent, and she was raised in Bedford, Texas. She is an associate professor of English at Tarrant County College in the Dallas–Fort Worth area, where she teaches creative writing.

She began as a poet. Her chapbook Ferry Crossing appeared in 2002 and her collection Palabras in Each Fist in 2009. Besides the Belpré Honor, The Other Half of Happy was named an ALA Notable Book and an Américas Award honor book, and it won the Texas Institute of Letters' Jean Flynn Award. Her second novel, Shine On, Luz Véliz! (Chronicle Books, 2022), was a Golden Kite Award finalist and won a Texas Institute of Letters prize. In 2023 she co-edited Boundless, a collection of stories celebrating multicultural and multiracial identities.
A Booklist review quoted on her site describes Quijana's worry about being "not Guatemalan enough."

2009: Palabras in Each Fist.
2019: The Other Half of Happy. 2020: Pura Belpré Author Honor.

people.name: Jennifer De Leon
body: Jennifer De Leon is a Boston-area author of young adult novels, beginning with Don't Ask Me Where I'm From (Simon & Schuster, 2020).

De Leon was born in the Boston area to Guatemalan parents. She earned a bachelor's degree at Connecticut College in international relations and French. During her Teach For America service she earned a master's in teaching at the University of San Francisco, and later she earned an MFA in creative writing at the University of Massachusetts Boston.

She is an associate professor at Framingham State University in Massachusetts and teaches in the Newport MFA program. Her books include a second young adult novel, Borderless (Simon & Schuster, 2023); the essay collection White Space: Essays on Culture, Race, & Writing (University of Massachusetts Press, 2021), which won the press's Juniper Prize; and Wise Latinas: Writers on Higher Education (University of Nebraska Press, 2014), an anthology she edited. She has held residencies or awards from Bread Loaf, Hedgebrook, Macondo, VONA and the Boston Public Library and was an artist-in-residence for the City of Boston.

She also founded Story Bridge, a program that brings people together to share their stories. The Guatemalan Center of New England named her keynote speaker for its January 2026 Quetzal Award Gala in Providence.
keyFacts: Born in the Boston area to Guatemalan parents.
2014: Edited Wise Latinas.
2020: Don't Ask Me Where I'm From.
2021: White Space, winner of the Juniper Prize.
2023: Borderless.

people.name: Rubio Rubín
body: In 2021, playing for Real Salt Lake, Rubio Rubín threw himself backward and struck a bicycle kick into the net against the San Jose Earthquakes. Major League Soccer later named it its 2021 Goal of the Year.

Rubín was born in March 1996 in Beaverton, Oregon, to a Guatemalan mother and a Mexican father. In 2012 he was named U.S. Soccer's Youth Player of the Year. From 2011 to 2015 he played 51 games for U.S. under-17, under-20 and under-23 teams and scored 20 goals. On November 14, 2014, at 18, he made his debut for the U.S. senior national team against Colombia. He went on to play seven senior games for the United States, all exhibition matches.
He played for FC Utrecht in the Netherlands (2014–2017), for clubs in Denmark and Norway, and for Tijuana and Dorados in Mexico. He joined Real Salt Lake for the 2021 season.

In 2022 FIFA approved his one-time request to switch his national team from the United States to Guatemala, his mother's birth country. Real Salt Lake quoted him saying that he wanted "to pursue my dream of playing in the World Cup." He played for the Charleston Battery in 2025, and on December 30, 2025, El Paso Locomotive FC of the USL Championship announced it had signed him.
keyFacts: March 1996: Born in Beaverton, Oregon, to a Guatemalan mother and Mexican father.
2012: U.S. Soccer Youth Player of the Year.
November 14, 2014: U.S. senior debut at 18; seven senior U.S. caps.
2021: MLS Goal of the Year.
2022: FIFA approved his switch to Guatemala's national team.

people.name: Silvia Quan
body: Silvia Quan is a Guatemalan disability rights expert. Disability Rights International describes her as a feminist and an expert on the rights of persons with disabilities. She took part in the UN Ad Hoc Committee that drafted and approved the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (2002–2006). From 2003 to 2013 she led the disability rights unit in Guatemala's human rights Ombudsman's Office.

From 2011 to 2016 she served as an independent expert on the UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, and was Vice-Chairperson in 2015–2016. She later worked as Senior Human Rights Advisor for the International Disability Alliance in Geneva (2017–2019). She has also consulted for HI (formerly Handicap International), CBM and the Disability Rights Fund.

She is President of Colectivo Vida Independiente de Guatemala. She is a senior consultant on an initiative to prevent violence against women and girls with disabilities and to improve their access to justice.
keyFacts: 2002–2006: Took part in the UN Ad Hoc Committee that drafted the disability rights convention.
2003–2013: Led the disability rights unit in Guatemala's Ombudsman's Office.
2011–2016: UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities; Vice-Chairperson 2015–2016.
2017–2019: Senior Human Rights Advisor, International Disability Alliance.

people.name: Antonio Palma López
people.field: Disability, youth and human rights advocacy
body: Antonio Palma López is a Guatemalan advocate for disability, youth and human rights. By the account of Diversability, which named him to its 2025 D-30 list, he began this work at 19 in student and national disability organizations. By 24 he had helped reform the statutes of RIADIS, the Latin American network of organizations of persons with disabilities. He founded its Youth Network and served as its Secretary of Human Rights and as its youth representative to the International Disability Alliance.

He led youth advocacy at regional and global disability summits and became the first young disabled person from the region to address the UN's ECOSOC Youth Forum. He advises the United Nations on its disability strategy. He co-founded Espacios Inclusivos, which works on disability inclusion across Latin America. He was named an outstanding UN volunteer in 2022, and the Congress of Guatemala recognized him as an inspiring young person in 2023.

institutions.name: The Guatemalan-Maya Center
institutions.type: Community nonprofit: health, education, cultural preservation
body: In the 1980s and 1990s, Maya refugees fleeing Guatemala's civil war arrived in Indiantown, Florida, and other farmworker communities in South Florida. Accounts differ on who to name as founders of the center that still operates in Lake Worth. WLRN reports that Father Frank O'Loughlin and Policarpia "Poli" Gaspar Xuncax founded it in 1992. CBS12 credits Father O'Loughlin and Guillermo Carrasco, a Colombian-born community leader who chairs the board, and reports that it was founded to help refugees navigate unfamiliar U.S. systems and keep their culture.

The center says it has served Indigenous Guatemalan-Maya and migrant families in Palm Beach County for more than 30 years. Its programs include Clínica Maya, which helps uninsured families get free or low-cost primary, specialty and prenatal care and goes with them to appointments to interpret language and culture. Clínica Maya works with University of Miami Health on cancer screenings and offers diabetes testing and nutrition education, including at gas stations where day laborers cash paychecks. The center also offers food and financial assistance and hosts heritage celebrations.

Its website reports more than 5,000 boxes of food distributed each month and more than 16,000 people served in 2025. CBS12 reports that it serves more than 1,000 families a month from more than 28 countries, and that its help is open to anyone in need. It does not serve Minnesota directly.
keyFacts: 1992: Founded in Lake Worth.
Clínica Maya: health access with language and cultural interpretation.
2025: More than 16,000 people served, by its own count.

institutions.name: Guatemalan Center of New England
body: The Guatemalan Center of New England holds an annual Quetzal Award Gala, named for Guatemala's national bird. For its 2026 gala, set for January 30 at the Marriott in Providence, the center announced it would honor Catarina Lorenzo, executive director of the Alliance to Mobilize Our Resistance (AMOR), for her immigrant-rights work. The author Jennifer De Leon was named keynote speaker, five students were to receive scholarships, and the program listed live music and cultural dance.

The center says its aim is to promote and share Guatemalan culture and to build cultural connections between Guatemala and New England. It also works to identify the needs of Guatemalans in the region and plan ways to meet them. Its programs include community events on education, the arts and cultural heritage, an annual cultural festival, workshops, and a scholarship program. Its site notes that Providence and Guatemala City signed a sister-city agreement in 2016.

Programs: cultural festival, workshops, scholarships.
2016: Providence and Guatemala City sister-city agreement.

institutions.name: International Mayan League
institutions.type: Indigenous Maya advocacy and cultural organization
body: On March 26, 2026, Juanita Cabrera López, executive director of the International Mayan League, presented the League's statement on Indigenous Peoples' rights and strict immigration policies at a roundtable with the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk.

By the League's own account, Maya refugees who had fled the war and genocide in Guatemala in the late 1970s and early 1980s founded it in 1991. It describes itself as a Maya organization that promotes, preserves and passes on Maya cosmovision (worldview), culture, history and traditional knowledge. It aims to address the root causes of discrimination, inequality and oppression of Maya people and the destruction of Maya communities and the environment. A University of Arizona event listing describes Cabrera López as Maya Mam from Guatemala's western highlands and a former political refugee.

Its programs cover Maya cosmovision, human rights and advocacy, environmental protection, immigration, a Maya Women Delegation, and a Gathering of Ancestral Wisdom. Its site also has an Indigenous language resources section.
keyFacts: 1991: Founded by Maya refugees from Guatemala's war.
Executive director: Juanita Cabrera López.
March 2026: Roundtable with the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.

institutions.name: Colectivo Vida Independiente de Guatemala
institutions.dates: Founded early this century, in its own words
body: In its own words, the Colectivo formed in Guatemala early this century. It grew from a group of people with and without disabilities involved in training and policy advocacy. Its goal is to change exclusionary structures in Guatemalan society through analysis, debate, training and research on the situation of disabled people, their families and their communities.

It says it has advocated before municipal authorities, Guatemala's Congress and the UN disability rights committee, trained public officials, and given legal support to disabled women who have experienced violence. With Disability Rights International it has followed a protective measure from the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights for patients of the Federico Mora psychiatric hospital.

In 2018 it co-published Todavía en peligro ("Still in Harm's Way") with Disability Rights International. The report covers international volunteer tourism, segregation and abuse of children in Guatemalan institutions. Silvia Quan is its president. It is based in Guatemala, not Minnesota.
keyFacts: Formed by people with and without disabilities.
2018: Co-published Todavía en peligro with Disability Rights International.

institutions.name: PACER Center
body: PACER Center in Bloomington is Minnesota's Parent Training and Information Center. Parents of children and youth with disabilities created it in 1977 to help other families make decisions about education and other services. It offers free individual help, workshops and publications.

In July 2024 PACER announced a 16-month project with Family Voices of Minnesota, funded by the Minnesota Department of Human Services, for Latino and Somali families of children on the autism spectrum. It created parent support groups led by Latino and Somali staff, held in Spanish and in Somali, with tip sheets and videos in English, Spanish and Somali.
PACER is a statewide Spanish-language starting point, and it is not specific to Guatemalan or Maya families. We found no record of Mayan-language services there.
keyFacts: 1977: Founded by parents of children and youth with disabilities.
Spanish-language advocates and materials.

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Guatemalan includes Ladino (mestizo) Spanish speakers and Maya people who speak one of more than 20 Mayan languages, who differ by faith, region, generation, schooling and time in the United States. We did not find a study of how Guatemalan or Maya families in Minnesota, or anywhere in the United States, understand disability. Most of what follows comes from one small study in rural Guatemala and two short sources.
questions: Which language do you speak best: Spanish, a Mayan language such as K'iche', Mam, Q'anjob'al, Ixil or Q'eqchi', or English?
Would you like a trained interpreter in that language? If one is hard to find, what should we do?
How do you and your family understand what is going on? If you want to share, what do you think caused it, and what have you already tried?
Who gave you a label or a diagnosis, and has it helped?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you, and what do you want it to avoid?
Who should be in the room, and who helps you make decisions?
Is faith, a church, or a healer part of how you handle this? Would you like services to work alongside that?
What do you most need right now, such as food, work, transportation or rent?
What would you like to know about who sees your information, including anything about immigration status?
What words do you use for your disability or condition, and what words do you not want us to use?
How would you like to get information: spoken, in writing, in pictures, or some other way?

context.heading: One study in rural Guatemala
body: Shaun Grech, for the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (2016), interviewed 27 disabled adults aged 18 to 67 and 6 family members in rural Guatemala, including mostly Indigenous areas. It is a small sample chosen through disability organizations, in another country, a decade ago. It says nothing about any one family in Minnesota.

Participants most often explained disability in Christian terms, as God's will or plan. Some Indigenous participants mentioned two older ideas, punishment for a parent's sin and the evil eye (mal de ojo) or a curse (maldición). Several said they did not hold these beliefs, or trusted a doctor's explanation more, and some said others had blamed a mother or father. Participants said poverty was their main concern: disability took its meaning from hunger, lost work and medical costs.

Family members, often mothers and other women, gave most of the care, and some left paid work to do it. Most participants also described kind, caring neighbors, especially in a crisis, and Grech calls these communities of support a key asset.

sources.label: Grech, Disability and Poverty in Rural Guatemala, London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (2016)

context.heading: Language, words and interpreters
body: In Grech's study, Indigenous participants without a mediator or translator in health facilities said they could barely explain themselves and were not heard, and described shame (vergüenza). Some stopped going back. Participants often did not know terms such as "person with a disability" and called themselves an ill or sick person (enfermo) or used "invalid" (inválido). The usual formal Spanish term is persona con discapacidad. Use the words the person uses.

We did not find documented disability terms in K'iche', Mam, Q'anjob'al or other Mayan languages. Ask a trained interpreter how a concept will be rendered, and check understanding. In a 2018 Christian Science Monitor article, interpreter Judy Jenner said relay interpretation, through Spanish, is like "playing the telephone game", and it was described there as a last resort.

sources.label: Grech, Disability and Poverty in Rural Guatemala (2016)
Christian Science Monitor, Indigenous language interpreters help asylum-seekers at the border (July 2, 2018)

context.heading: Stigma and when people seek help
body: A 2019 student case study of a special education school in Nebaj, in the Ixil region of Quiché, reports stigma against people with physical, intellectual and developmental disabilities. It says some families feel shame and hesitate to take children out in public or enroll them in school. By that account the school, founded in 2002, serves more than 30 students.

A 2019 case study from Asociación Grupo Ermita Alzheimer de Guatemala calls dementia a taboo among Indigenous peoples in Guatemala and says people usually seek help only when it is far advanced. Its example is one Kaqchikel family who first suspected witchcraft. The author also says many adults speak only an Indigenous language, and that some families travel 8 to 10 hours to reach the association. It is one association's account and one case.

sources.label: Pomp and Dunlevy, International Undergraduate Journal for Service-Learning, Leadership, and Social Change (2019)
López Murga, Stigma and response to dementia in Guatemala's Indigenous population, Alzheimer's Disease International (2019)

context.heading: Healers, faith and formal services
body: Grech reports that healers remain widely used in the Indigenous areas he studied: curanderos (folk healers), guías espirituales (spiritual guides) and sobadores, who heal through massage. They help give meaning to illness and are cheaper and closer than Western medicine, which he says can delay or replace formal care. He also describes Catholic and Evangelical churches as strong and growing, and in isolated areas often more present than government or health services. Ask what a person already does, and plan alongside it with their consent.

sources.label: Grech, Disability and Poverty in Rural Guatemala (2016)

context.heading: What we could not find
body: We found no research documenting who makes decisions in Guatemalan or Maya households, so ask each person. We found no organization in Minnesota specific to Guatemalan or Maya disabled people and their families, though the search was limited. Fear of an agency can be about protecting a relative in a mixed-status family, the situation Delia Ramirez describes in her own family. Before reading a missed appointment as a cultural matter, check for that, and for shifts, transportation and cost.

communityRoutes.name: Discapacitados Abriéndose Caminos (D.A.C.)
communityRoutes.purpose: A South St. Paul nonprofit whose Spanish-language website says it guides families with a disabled child, adult or relative through health, county, community and school systems. The site also describes a weekly support group, trainings, help at hospital appointments and home visits, but its latest dated item is from December 2015, so call to ask what runs now. Federal tax records show the group is still operating: it filed its 2025 return in May 2026. It is not specific to Guatemalan or Maya families, so ask about Mayan-language interpreting.

communityRoutes.name: CIELO Center for Indigenous Language and Power
communityRoutes.purpose: Trains interpreters in Indigenous languages for migrants from Mexico and Guatemala. It is based in Los Angeles and is a place to ask about finding a Mayan-language interpreter.

organizations.intro: Guatemalan Minnesotans live in Worthington, where the Black Christ of Esquipulas feast at St. Mary's has drawn hundreds, and elsewhere in the state; people came from as far as St. Cloud to a 2022 consular visit in Worthington. Guatemala's foreign ministry, as reported by Plaza Pública in February 2026, counts 19,378 Guatemalans in Minnesota; we did not find how that figure was produced, and the state has no Guatemalan consulate. We found no standalone Guatemalan or Maya association in Minnesota and no source naming the Maya languages spoken here. What is documented runs through parishes, consular visits and Latino organizing and service groups. This list is a starting point for learning, is not complete, and says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.name: St. Mary's Catholic Church (Worthington)
entries.purpose: Parish where hundreds gathered in January 2025 for the Black Christ of Esquipulas feast. Families raised nearly $40,000 over three years for a carved replica of the crucifix and marimbas from Guatemala. The parish has Spanish-language Masses and choirs. AP's story names San Marcos, in Guatemala, as the home region of parishioners it interviewed, and reports that villages there held the same feast that week.
entries.linkLabel: AP news story via CBS Minnesota; we did not find a parish website

entries.name: Consulate General of Guatemala in Omaha
entries.location: Omaha, Nebraska, with mobile visits to Minnesota
entries.purpose: Minnesota has no Guatemalan consulate. Mobile visits by the Omaha consulate were held in Worthington in March 2026, and a mobile consulate came to Austin in August 2026. The Chicago consulate ran earlier visits: Minneapolis in 2019, and Worthington in 2022, when it processed paperwork for 759 people. Mobile visits offer passports, birth certificates and some civil registry services, but not the national ID (DPI). Call before relying on a date.
entries.linkLabel: Embassy of Guatemala, list of consulates

entries.name: Worthington Community Education (ISD 518)
entries.purpose: The public school district's community education program. It provided space and coordinated volunteers for the 2022 Guatemalan mobile consulate.

entries.name: CLUES (Comunidades Latinas Unidas En Servicio)
entries.location: St. Paul, Minneapolis, Willmar and Austin
entries.purpose: Founded in 1981 and calls itself Minnesota's largest Latino-led nonprofit. Offers behavioral health care, job training, elder programs, and family wellness and childcare programs, in Spanish and English. As of October 2026 its president and CEO is Liliana Letran-Garcia.

entries.name: COPAL (Comunidades Organizando el Poder y la Acción Latina)
aliases: Communities Organizing Latine Power and Action
entries.type: Advocacy, mutual aid and workers' center
entries.purpose: A member-based Latine organization founded in 2018. Its work includes health and wellness, a workers' center for wage recovery and unemployment benefits, rental assistance, rural resource access in southern Minnesota, and voter engagement. It is the Minnesota member of Alianza Americas.

entries.name: Unidos MN
entries.purpose: A grassroots organization of Minnesota's working families, working on immigration, education and climate justice. Its site posts driver's license help, Know Your Rights resources and Guatemalan mobile consulate dates. Named among groups meeting community needs in Worthington in 2022.

entries.name: Minnesota Seeds of Justice
entries.purpose: A nonprofit that says it works toward healthy rural communities by strengthening local leadership, investing in community-led solutions and building partnerships. Sahan Journal and MPR News described it in 2022 as a collective supporting leaders of color, immigrants and refugees.

entries.name: Voices for Racial Justice
entries.purpose: Works on education equity, community-centered policy making, and democracy and civic engagement. Its site offers a 2026–27 parent fellowship and safety-planning resources for immigrant families. Named as working in Worthington in 2022.

entries.name: Ascension Catholic Church (Iglesia Ascensión)
entries.purpose: Parish with bilingual announcements that hosted a Guatemalan mobile consulate in September 2019. We found no Guatemalan-specific group there.

entries.name: Sagrado Corazón de Jesús (Minneapolis)
entries.purpose: A Spanish-language Catholic chaplaincy located at Incarnation parish, by the archdiocese's listing. We found no Guatemalan-specific group or Esquipulas feast there, so it is listed as a broader Latino contact.

entries.name: Our Lady of Guadalupe Catholic Church (St. Paul)
entries.purpose: A West Side parish with Masses in Spanish and English. We found no Guatemalan-specific ministry there.

entries.name: La Prensa de Minnesota (LCN Media)
entries.purpose: Local, national, Mexican and world news and entertainment for Minnesota Latinos.

entries.name: dglobe.com (Worthington newspaper)
entries.purpose: The local paper for Nobles County, including coverage of Guatemalan residents such as an August 2024 piece on a Guatemalan immigrant and a fourth-generation farmer.

entries.name: Sahan Journal
entries.purpose: Covers Minnesota immigrant communities, including Worthington, unaccompanied Central American minors, and profiles of southwest Minnesota immigrant families.

entries.name: MPR News
entries.purpose: Has reported on Worthington's Guatemalan and Latino residents.

entries.name: Telemundo Minnesota
entries.purpose: Carries Telemundo network programming plus Minnesota programming on low-power stations in the St. Cloud–St. Paul, Rochester and Duluth areas, as of an August 2025 report. It does not reach Worthington over the air.
entries.linkLabel: NorthPine trade report; we did not find a station website

entries.name: Univision Minnesota (WUMN-LD)
entries.purpose: The station's own site calls it Univision-affiliated and was posting local news in October 2026.

entries.name: Alianza Americas
entries.purpose: A network of more than 55 Latin American and Caribbean immigrant-led and immigrant-serving organizations in 18 states and Washington, D.C. Its Minnesota member is COPAL.

entries.name: CARECEN Los Angeles (Central American Resource Center)
entries.location: Los Angeles, Van Nuys and San Bernardino
entries.purpose: Low-cost immigration legal services, organizing and policy advocacy, a day labor center, and Know Your Rights workshops for Central Americans, including Guatemalans. Other CARECENs, such as in Washington, D.C., are separate groups.

entries.name: CIELO (Comunidades Indígenas en Liderazgo)
entries.purpose: Works with Indigenous migrants. Its Center for Indigenous Language and Power trains Indigenous-language interpreters, linked to demand from migrants from Mexico and Guatemala, and it hosts a national Indigenous interpreters conference.

entries.name: Prensa Libre
entries.purpose: Has a topic page on Guatemalan migrants in the United States, covering deportations, consular services and migration policy, with items from October 2026.

entries.name: Soy502
entries.purpose: A national news site covering politics, security, community, sports and entertainment in Guatemala. It has no dedicated migrant section.

entries.name: ICRC radio spots in Guatemalan Indigenous languages
entries.location: International Committee of the Red Cross
entries.purpose: Short audio spots with practical safety advice for migrants in Mam, K'iche', Q'eqchi' and Kaqchikel, among others. The 2015 material is one of the few ready-made audio sources we found in Mam.

entries.name: Agencia Ocote
entries.purpose: Launched in March 2019. Covers women and diversity, human rights, historical memory and justice, the environment and democracy, with a podcast and the fact-checking unit Fáctica.

entries.name: Plaza Pública
entries.purpose: Guatemalan investigative and analytical journalism, including a February 2026 report on Guatemalans in Minnesota.
